Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether individuals can view their data held in the ID database and see how it has been accessed
Comments: Law 22/11 (Data Protection Act) grants data subjects rights of access, rectification, cancellation and objection. However, the World Bank ID4D Diagnostic (2024) notes that access to the BI platform for online user identification is not accessible for all Angolans, and the SEPE portal requires BI/NIF numbers for account access. No evidence was found of a dedicated individual portal or mechanism enabling citizens to view the personal data held in the PGIBI ID database. The right exists in law but practical digital access to one's own ID records is not operationally implemented.

Definition: Whether the system enables Know Your Customer (KYC) packet collection for service provision, particularly financial services
Comments: The BI national ID enables KYC for regulated entities in Angola. The National ID (BI) is the primary document for customer identity verification by banks, financial institutions, and telecoms. The NIF (tax number) equals the BI number, facilitating KYC. Law No. 34/11 and Law No. 3/14 establish core KYC obligations; BNA Directives 01/2025 and 02/2025 define new standards for onboarding. The World Bank diagnostic confirms PGIBI is linked to banking databases for verification. Fintech solutions like Xikila Money use BI document scanning and biometric data collection for mobile financial services.

Definition: Whether the ID authority and system are subject to general oversight of the courts and judicial review
Value Name: Yes, but not specific to ID
Comments: Angola's Constitution (2010) guarantees the right to identity, privacy and habeas data (Article 32), providing a basis for judicial recourse. The general court system has jurisdiction over disputes involving personal data and identity rights. However, no ID-specific judicial mechanisms were identified in the research. Law 22/11 (Data Protection) provides for enforcement and sanctions by the APD, with standard judicial review available but no dedicated ID tribunal or court.

Definition: Whether the civil registration and digital ID systems are integrated
Comments: There is partial integration between civil registration and the national ID system. Birth registration is a prerequisite for obtaining the BI card, and the RCI (civil registration) system assigns a Unique Citizen Number (NUC) that feeds into the PGIBI ID database. The 2019 Civil Registration and Identity Card Attribution Project launched the Integrated Civil and Criminal Identification Management Platform (PGIBI) to increase coverage rates. However, the World Bank ID4D Diagnostic notes they remain separate systems; full automation to eliminate breeder documents is planned but not yet achieved. Legacy paper-based records also limit full integration.

Definition: Whether procedural rules for collection, storage, and sharing of ID-related personal data are publicly available and established
Comments: Angola has partial data sharing rules. Law 22/11 establishes data sharing principles requiring APD notification/authorisation for data interconnection. Presidential Decree 46/18 (PNAGIA) provides a framework for data and information sharing between government agencies. The PGIBI provides controlled access to the ID database for entities such as migration services and banks. However, implementation of PNAGIA is still work in progress and not all government services have been integrated. The World Bank diagnostic notes gaps in data sharing governance including absence of full privacy-by-design requirements.

Definition: Whether specific regulation or policy addresses digital ID beyond general identification legislation
Comments: While Angola has Law 4/09 (and amendments) governing the national ID card (Bilhete de Identidade) and Presidential Decree 202/11 on electronic signatures, there is no specific standalone Digital ID regulation. The World Bank ID4D Diagnostic (2024) notes that Angola plans to introduce a digital ID solution and recommends updating the legal framework for privacy-by-design, PKI standards and digital ID. A draft AI law and amendment to the Data Protection Act are in progress but no dedicated Digital ID law exists.

Definition: Whether national data protection legislation exists and covers personal data linked to the ID system
Comments: Angola enacted Law 22/11 on the Protection of Personal Data on 17 June 2011, making it one of 36 African countries with a Data Protection Act. The law establishes data processing principles (transparency, lawfulness, proportionality, purpose, accuracy), regulates sensitive data (including biometric/genetic data), and requires notification/authorisation by the Data Protection Agency (APD). Angola also ratified the Malabo Convention. A draft amendment to the DPA is in progress to address AI and digital ID.

Definition: Whether a Data Protection Authority or similar body regulates ID data collection and sharing by the ID system
Comments: The Angolan Data Protection Agency (Agência de Proteção de Dados, APD) was formally constituted in 2016 (some sources cite October 2019 as when it became operational) under Law 22/11 to oversee collection and processing of personal data, enforce data protection legislation and apply sanctions. The APD has intensified supervisory activities in recent years and has levied significant financial fines against non-compliant organisations. It is responsible for approving international data transfers and authorising processing of sensitive data.

Definition: Whether the digital ID credential serves as legal proof of an individual's identity as codified in law
Comments: The Bilhete de Identidade (BI) serves as the primary legal proof of identity in Angola. Under Law 4/09 (and amendments), the BI is required to access numerous public services including education, employment, bank accounts, property registration, vehicle registration, loans, and voting. Birth registration is mandatory to obtain the BI. The BI constitutes legally recognised proof of identity and nationality for Angolan citizens.

Definition: Whether formal legislation (act, law, regulation) governs digital identity including identification acts, digital ID laws, or equivalent legislation
Comments: Angola has a comprehensive legal framework for identification including: Law 4/09 (amended by Laws 20/17 and 3/21) - Legal Regime of Civil Identification mandating chip, unique citizen number (NUC) and biometrics; Law 22/11 - Data Protection Law; Law 7/17 - Cybersecurity/Network and IT Systems Protection Law; Presidential Decree 202/11 - Regulation of Information Society Technologies and Services; Presidential Decree 46/18 (PNAGIA) - national interoperability plan. Angola's Constitution (Article 32) protects personal privacy.

Definition: Whether the system and the production of credentials can be managed, maintained and developed by in-country technical staff (as opposed to foreign vendors)
Comments: The World Bank ID4D Diagnostic (2024) notes limited domestic maintenance capacity, with vendor lock-in to private firms for the RCI and PGIBI systems (DGM Sistemas, HID Global, Unisys Africa - foreign/private vendors). The PGIBI civil registration system was developed by CEIEC (Chinese consultancy). The 2023 biometric passport contract was awarded to ANY Security Printing Company (Hungary-based) for USD 139M over 10 years. The diagnostic recommends cloud hosting, staff training and SOPs to build in-country capacity. This represents partial in-country capacity.

Definition: Whether the Ministry of Finance has oversight of the financing and development of the digital ID system
Comments: The Ministry of Justice and Human Rights (MINJUSDH) and the Administrative Modernization Institute (IMA) oversee the ID and digital ID strategy respectively. The Ministry of Finance has partial oversight through general government budget allocation processes. The World Bank Angola Digital Acceleration Project (P180693) involves fiduciary oversight mechanisms. However, no evidence was found of dedicated Ministry of Finance-specific oversight mechanisms for the ID system beyond general government financial management. The ID system financing involves both government budget and external funding (World Bank, India credit line).

Definition: Whether the ongoing management, maintenance and development of the ID system can be funded by sustainable domestic resources
Comments: The Angola ID system relies on mixed domestic and external funding. External funding sources include the World Bank Angola Digital Acceleration Project (P180693), a $200M credit line from India (2025) for DPI development (digital ID modelled on Aadhaar), and the $139M contract with ANY Security Printing Company (Hungary) for biometric passports. Domestic government funds finance MINJUSDH operations and the PGIBI platform. The first issuance of ID cards and birth certificates is free (domestic subsidy). The system is therefore characterised by mixed domestic/external funding.

Definition: Whether identity records are stored in electronic/digital format versus paper-based records
Comments: Angola has a centralised PGIBI electronic database (production centre in Luanda) for the national ID (BI). However, the World Bank ID4D Diagnostic (2024) notes that most civil registration and identification records are maintained in unindexed, paper-based databases. The birth registration process remains primarily paper-based but is being digitalized, with computer equipment progressively rolled out in Luanda, provincial capitals, and 34 maternity wards. This reflects a mix of paper and digital systems.

Definition: Whether the digital ID system is designed to be interoperable across government agencies and with other systems through APIs or data exchange protocols
Comments: The PGIBI (Plataforma de Gestão Integrada da Identificação Civil e Criminal) is integrated with civil registration (RCI/SIRC), social security, tax (NIF), and electoral register. The BI card platform allows interoperability with several public platforms including banks (BAI, BMA) and SEPE (Portal dos Serviços Públicos Electrónicos). Presidential Decree 46/18 approved PNAGIA (National Plan for Global Architecture for Interoperability of Central and Local State Administration) mandating data/information sharing between government agencies. Full implementation of PNAGIA is still in progress.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for opening bank accounts and accessing financial services
Comments: The Bilhete de Identidade (BI) is mandatory for opening a bank account and requesting loans in Angola. The World Bank ID4D Diagnostic and the Paradigm Initiative policy brief both confirm that the BI is a prerequisite for opening a bank account. The KYC/AML regulatory framework (Laws 34/11 and 3/14, BNA Directives 01/2025 and 02/2025) mandates BI verification for customer onboarding by all regulated financial institutions. The NIF equals the BI number, embedding it in the financial system. Limited coverage (46% BI penetration) means those without BI are excluded from banking services.

Definition: Whether credentials are issued free of charge
Comments: The first issuance of the Bilhete de Identidade is free for all ages under Law 3/21 (and previously free for ages 6-11 under Law 4/09). Birth certificates are also free for first issuance. Renewals cost 455 AKZ (~USD 0.50) and duplicates 3,828 AKZ (~USD 4.50). The Greater Internet Freedom report (2023) confirms Angola has not increased the cost of IDs (though passport costs rose significantly). The free first issuance policy makes the credential accessible at no cost for initial enrollment.

Definition: Age in years at which an individual becomes eligible to register for digital ID
Comments: Under Law 4/09 as originally enacted, national IDs were mandated from age 10. Law 3/21 (2021 amendment) removed the minimum age requirement, making the ID available to all ages including newborns. A November 2025 initiative began issuing ID cards to newborns in Zaire Province. Law 4/09 specifies the first issuance is free for applicants aged 6-11. The enrollment eligibility of 6-10 years (category 3) is supported; with the 2021 amendment opening it to younger ages.

Definition: Whether registration for digital ID is mandatory, optional, or mandatory for specific groups
Comments: Under Law 4/09, the Bilhete de Identidade is mandatory for Angolan nationals when required for legal purposes (employment, banking, voting, property). Birth registration is mandatory under law. However, not all citizens are compelled by law to enrol proactively - the ID is required when accessing specific services rather than being an unconditional universal obligation at birth for all ages. The 2021 amendment began extending it to newborns, representing mandatory registration for some groups in specific contexts.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for accessing public healthcare services
Comments: The World Bank ID4D Diagnostic (2024) notes that no ID is required for healthcare access (paper/digital patient IDs are used). However, the 2025 newborn ID initiative is linked to the 'Born with a birth certificate' programme supported by the Ministry of Health and UNICEF, aiming to issue ID cards at birth alongside birth certificates to improve healthcare tracking and service access. The diagnostic recommends linking the health system to the CR/ID for a health number at birth and patient monitoring. Current healthcare access does not require the BI but the ID is used/accepted in healthcare administration contexts.

Definition: Whether non-nationals including refugees, asylum seekers, and permanent residents are eligible to register
Comments: The Bilhete de Identidade (BI) is for Angolan nationals only. However, foreigners residing in Angola are eligible for a Residence Permit, and refugees receive a Refugee Card. The civil registration system records all births including those of foreigners and stateless individuals. The 2025 newborn ID programme noted measures to prevent registration of foreigners near the DRC border, indicating the BI is restricted to nationals, but other ID documents are available to some non-nationals (residence permits/refugee cards).

Definition: Percentage of eligible population that has been issued or registered with digital ID credentials
Comments: According to the UN Centre of Excellence for CRVS and the World Bank ID4D Diagnostic (2024), in 2022 approximately 46% of Angolan citizens had an ID card (BI). The Paradigm Initiative policy brief (2024) notes 14 million out of 33 million Angolans (approximately 42%) hold an identity card. The World Bank 2017 data cited 28% biometric national ID coverage. Birth registration stands at 77% (2022 UN data). The 46% BI coverage places Angola in the 20-49% range.

Definition: Whether ID system undergoes regular security audits, penetration testing, or vulnerability assessments
Comments: Law 7/17 (Network and IT Systems Protection Law) mandates incident response and security measures for electronic communications operators including notification to APD and INACOM upon security breaches. The World Bank ID4D Diagnostic (2024) notes that PGIBI has security measures against unauthorised access but identifies gaps in critical information infrastructure protection (CIIP), including the absence of a formal Computer Incident Response Team (CIRT). The diagnostic recommends threat modelling, audits and tamper-proof logs. While formal security requirements are established in law, comprehensive independent security reviews of the ID system have not been publicly documented.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for SIM card activation and mobile service registration
Comments: SIM card registration is mandatory in Angola. The Greater Internet Freedom country report (2023) states that Angolans require a national ID card for SIM registration, while foreigners require a passport with valid visa. The World Bank ID4D Diagnostic confirms mobile SIM registration requires the BI, with a limit of 20 SIMs per person per operator (up to 60 total). This constitutes mandatory use of national ID for SIM card registration.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for registering for social assistance programs and accessing social services
Comments: The national ID (BI) is required for accessing social services in Angola. The World Bank ID4D Diagnostic confirms the Unified Social Register (CSU) is interoperable with the ID system and uses BI/birth certificate for beneficiaries of the Kwenda cash transfer programme. The BI is also required for education enrolment, municipal administrative services, and paying municipal fees. The Paradigm Initiative report notes that limited ID coverage means those without identity cards are excluded from accessing services.
